## Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author)

I work on Quaternary paleoclimate reconstructions and with Earth system scientists, and can comment on the relevance and impact of this study. It is indeed assumed by many that humans have played a significant and increasing role in shaping Holocene vegetation assemblage dynamics for the 8.5 to 2 ka BP study interval. This assumption is relevant, for instance, to the vigorous debate about whether the Anthropocene should be viewed as having gradually unfolded over tens of millennia (the “Anthropocene event” of Gibbard et al., 2022; see also the gradualist depiction in fig. 1 of Ellis, 2023), or whether significant impacts are restricted to more recent times. The conclusion that humans were not responsible for broad-scale ecological processes during this interval of study is therefore important to this debate, and it sets a baseline for human-driven impacts that were to later overwhelm Earth system functioning.

The study itself is based on the novel statistical analysis of two very large and independent data sets. The conclusions seem to be well supported by the data, and careful thought is given to explaining their limitations. There is one controversial aspect of Holocene climate that is not addressed but perhaps could be. It concerns claims by Ruddiman et al. (e.g. 2003, 2007, 2020) that the emergence of intensive rice cultivation in eastern Asia was responsible for the release of significant carbon dioxide and methane into the atmosphere, from 7 ka and 5 ka respectively. This would explain why global temperatures remain relatively flat even as summer insolation at 65°N declined from its peak in the Early Holocene. These claims have been questioned by Zalasiewicz et al. (2024) who noted that isotopic and modelling studies are consistent with oceanic outgassing rather than anthropogenic causes for these rises in greenhouse gases. Moreover, Summerhayes et al. (2024) noted that global average insolation may have in fact risen slightly over the past 7 kyr, potentially leading to the degassing of the global ocean which is by far the largest CO2 reservoir on the planet. The question then, as to whether there is evidence within the pollen record for substantial cultivation of rice in eastern Asia, becomes relevant in assessing the extent of human impacts on the Earth system.

> **Response.** We thank the reviewer for placing the study within the debate over early human influence on the Earth system. The history of rice cultivation in eastern Asia is clearly relevant to the early anthropogenic hypothesis. Our evidence, however, cannot resolve that question. The ten pollen assemblage properties describe broad changes in richness, evenness, and compositional reorganisation; they do not identify rice pollen or reconstruct the extent and intensity of cultivation. Nor do the present models examine greenhouse-gas sources. Consequently, the larger estimated climatic contribution in our analyses neither supports nor refutes the proposal that early rice agriculture affected atmospheric carbon dioxide or methane. A direct test would require harmonised taxon-level rice evidence, regional histories of cultivation and land use, and an analytical design linking those histories to greenhouse-gas change.

> **Changes in the revised article.** The final Discussion paragraph now locates the result within the early anthropogenic debate while defining its evidential boundary. It explains why broad pollen assemblage properties cannot substitute for rice-pollen records, archaeological histories of cultivation, or evidence concerning the sources of Holocene greenhouse gases.

I consider the MS to be publishable after minor revision, and perhaps following consideration of the question of eastern Asia rice cultivation. The Holocene is crucial to our understanding of the rise of civilizations and the emergence of the modern world. This MS will have a profound impact on the way we approach these fundamental issues.

Martin J. Head  
5 July 2025

> **Response.** We thank the reviewer for this assessment. The revised article now discusses eastern-Asian rice cultivation as an important historical and Earth-system question while making clear that the present broad-scale pollen analysis cannot adjudicate between competing explanations of Holocene greenhouse-gas change.

> **Response.** We thank the reviewer for this literature. It is now used to frame the early anthropogenic debate and the alternative anthropogenic and oceanic explanations for Holocene greenhouse-gas change. We state explicitly that the evidence analysed here does not distinguish between those mechanisms.

### Minor detailed comments on the MS

Line 69. Should there be consistency here in the precision, i.e. 8.5–2.0 ka BP? See Line 336 where this consistency is maintained.

> **Response.** Agreed. We now use 8.5–2.0 ka BP consistently when specifying the study interval.

Line 82. For land use, reference to Our World in Data would be better: <https://ourworldindata.org/land-use>.

> **Response.** Thank you for the suggestion. We added the Our World in Data synthesis to document the long-term expansion of cropland, grazing land, and settlements. Peer-reviewed studies remain the basis for causal interpretations and for the geological discussion of the Anthropocene.

Line 95. not “middle Holocene” but “Middle Holocene” if you are referring to the formal substage/subepoch (8.2–4.2 ka), or “mid-Holocene” if more loosely.

> **Response.** Corrected. We use “Middle Holocene” for the formal subdivision and “mid-Holocene” for informal usage.

Line 113. Pleistocene and Holocene epochs (not periods).

> **Response.** Corrected to “epochs.”

Line 116. “the term “period” not needed here because the Holocene can only refer to a unit of time.

> **Response.** Corrected. We removed the unnecessary use of “period” with Holocene.

Line 124. reflects, not reflect (“each” refers to the singular).

> **Response.** Corrected to “reflects.”

Line 134. “on the period between 8.5 and 2.0 ka BP” if the consistency in precision is justified.

> **Response.** Corrected, with the study interval consistently expressed as 8.5–2.0 ka BP or “between 8.5 and 2.0 ka BP,” according to sentence structure.

Line 147. we would expect an altered covariance between the PAPs within different climate zones on continental regions.

> **Response.** Corrected and clarified. H2 is now expressed as a prediction about historical changes in the relationships among pollen assemblage properties within continental groups and their regions, rather than as a claim about the response of particular plant taxa.

Line 150. This subheading is a little confusing because while it references H1, it describes the result rather than the stated hypothesis. I realize that restating the hypothesis could be misleading here, so perhaps frame the hypothesis as “H1: Holocene palaeoclimate versus human impact”.

> **Response.** Agreed. We revised the subheading to “H1: Holocene human impact secondary to palaeoclimate,” thereby linking the hypothesis to its ecological and temporal setting while indicating the observed direction of the result.

Line 157. Middle to Late Holocene – you are referring to official subseries of the Holocene, so the first initial of the modifiers “middle” and “late” must be capitalized. If this is not done, you will need to define what will then be informal terms.

> **Response.** Corrected to “Middle to Late Holocene” where the formal subdivisions are intended.

Line 175. Again an issue of consistency in precision. In Asia 3.5 ka BP so for Europe should that be 3.0 ka BP?

> **Response.** Corrected. Ages are now reported with consistent precision within each comparison.

Line 218. palaeoclimate data between 8.5 and 2.0 ka BP to invesitgate … (then delete “8.5 and 2.0 ka BP” at the end of the sentence).

> **Response.** Corrected and the duplicated interval was removed.

Line 220. Our first hypothesis posited that …

> **Response.** Corrected. The sentence now begins with an explicit formulation of the first hypothesis.

Line 241. PAPs not PAPS.

> **Response.** Corrected throughout to “PAPs.”

Line 275. “mid” is not a stand-alone word in most dictionaries, so it would be “mid-Holocene” as an informal interval of time.

> **Response.** Corrected to “mid-Holocene.”

Line 326. “factors like” better as “such factors as”.

> **Response.** Corrected to “such factors as.”

Line 336. “from 8.5 to 2.0 ka BP”. Use an en-dash when referring to, but not specifying, a range, such as “over the range 8.5–2.0 ka BP”. I note here that “2.0 ka unlike elsewhere is states to two significant figures, which seems appropriate precision if supported by the dates themselves.

> **Response.** Corrected. We use “from 8.5 to 2.0 ka BP” in prose and an en dash in the adjectival or compact range “8.5–2.0 ka BP.”

Line 467. You do make it clear that Eric C Grimm is no longer with us, but are you perhaps dedicating this MS to the memory of the person rather than the person themselves? Remember to change “manuscript” to “article” when revising the MS.

> **Response.** Corrected. The article is now dedicated to the memory of Eric C. Grimm, and submission-facing prose refers to the revised work as an article.
